articles.title: I'm a trained barista, and these are the top 3 milk frothers I recommend for faultless lattes — with no special techniques involved
articles.text:
Want delicious lattes the easy way? I'm a certified barista, and these are the top 3 milk frothers I recommend for perfect results every time
Want to make delicious lattes and cappuccinos at home without using a steam wand? You need an electric milk frother — and as TechRadar's resident barista, I've put together the top three I recommend, whether you enjoy plant milk or dairy.
Before we get started, I should note that electric milk frothers and steam wands both have their pros and cons. A manual steam wand works much more quickly than an electric milk frother, and once you've got your eye in, it allows you greater control over the texture of the milk (more creamy for lattes, and 'drier' for a cappuccino, for example).
Electric frothers, however, can usually whip up cold milk foam as well as hot, and make it easy to prepare other drinks including hot chocolate and protein shakes. The inside of an electric milk frother usually has a non-stick coating, making it a breeze to clean. An electric frother is also a great option if you have limited mobility, often featuring just one or two physical buttons that can be operated with one hand. Sounds good? On with the recommendations...
Dreo Baristamaker
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
If you enjoy plant-based milk, the Dreo Baristamaker is the electric milk frother for you. While the other two in this guide are optimized for dairy, the Baristamaker also has settings for soya, almond, coconut, and oat — as well as half-and-half if you want something richer in your coffee.
The base of the unit contains the heating element and motor, and the two whisking attachments are held in position (and spun) using magnets. One attachment looks like your standard milk whisk, while the other has large blades to pull the milk in towards the center, where a mesh screen breaks up large bubbles and turns them into fine foam.
During the foaming process, the Baristamaker will alternate between stirring and foaming, which is intended to create an even texture. It's also the only electric milk frother here whose pitcher has a fine spout, which is essential for creating latte art, though in my tests I found that the foam was less smooth than milk steamed the old-fashioned way, and I couldn't achieve the same results when pouring it.
Nevertheless, for sheer versatility, the Baristamaker is my number one pick if you're looking for an electric milk frother, provided your budget can take the hit. If you're looking for something a little more affordable (or just smaller), read on for two more options.

The Smeg Mini Milk Frother is an ideal companion to the Lavazza A Modo Mio Smeg capsule coffee machine, but its clean, minimalist design would look right at home anywhere (particularly since it comes in a wide array of colors, including black, white, and pastels).
Its controls are extremely simple: just one button on the front, which you press once, twice, or three times to choose your preferred setting (hot milk foam, hot milk, or cold milk foam). There are no options for different milk types, and according to Smeg, it's intended to be used with chilled full-fat dairy milk, which it turns into quite a thick foam. I also tried it with barista-style oat and almond milk to see how it compared with the Baristamaker; oat milk produced similar results to dairy, while almond was 'drier' and less creamy.
Whether I used the hot milk or hot milk foam option, the milk was always heated to exactly 140F / 60C, which is optimal for coffee. However, it's a shame the milk vessel doesn't have a fine spout like the Baristamaker; the milk pours cleanly without drips, but the lack of fine control combined with the thick texture means it's impossible to create latte art.

Philips Baristina Milk Frother
This smart-looking electric milk frother is available on its own, or bundled with the Philips Baristina coffee machine — one of my all-time favorite espresso machines. When my colleague Max Langridge tested this frother, he found it "consistently produces thick milk foam, whether hot or cold", but as with all the devices we've tried, the foam it produces tends to be on the stiffer side and not ideal for pouring latte art.
Unlike the other frothers here, the Baristina doesn't use a heating element underneath the pitcher to heat your milk. Instead, it has a heated coil, which needs to be removed first if you want your milk cold. There's no audible beep to tell you that your milk is ready, but there is an LED indicator, and at just 40dB the while heating and whisking process is very quiet.
There are no options for tweaking the texture of your finished froth, but unlike the Smeg Mini Milk Frother above, Philips says that the Baristina frother is designed to be used with all types of milk — plant and dairy. However, Max noticed that whatever type of milk he used, the foam was always on the thicker side, and like the Smeg frother, there's no spout for pouring patterns onto your coffee.
If you're considering the Baristina coffee maker and milk frother bundle, you should also be aware that Philips has recently launched the Baristina Latte, which bundles both into one compact package. I've not had the opportunity to test it yet, but I have high expectations.

articles.title: Dónde veo la papelera de WhatsApp para eliminar fotos, videos, audios y documentos
articles.text:
Para encontrar la papelera de WhatsApp, basta con dirigirse a ‘Ajustes’, seguir a ‘Almacenamiento y datos’ y luego a ‘Administración de almacenamiento’.
Después ir al apartado que se encuentra debajo de ‘Revisa y elimina elementos’. Para eliminar un elemento, solo hay que pulsar la opción ‘Seleccionar’, elegir los archivos deseados y tocar el ícono de la papelera.
PUBLICIDAD
Por qué es útil la papelera de WhatsApp
La papelera de WhatsApp es útil porque funciona como un espacio de “almacenamiento intermedio” en el que se acumulan fotos, videos, audios y documentos que parecían borrados, pero que todavía siguen ocupando memoria en el celular.
Vaciarla permite liberar espacio de manera rápida: con el tiempo, esos archivos “olvidados” pueden sumar una cantidad considerable de almacenamiento y afectar el rendimiento del teléfono o incluso el funcionamiento de la propia aplicación.
PUBLICIDAD
Además, esta sección también sirve para otra necesidad común: recuperar un archivo eliminado por error antes de borrarlo de forma definitiva.
Por eso, revisar y limpiar esta “papelera” con regularidad ayuda a mantener WhatsApp más liviano y el dispositivo mejor optimizado.
De qué otras formas ahorrar espacio en WhatsApp
Además de vaciar la “papelera” (Administración de almacenamiento), en WhatsApp podés ahorrar espacio de estas formas:
- Revisar los chats de grupos.
Suelen generar un volumen alto de fotos, videos, GIF, stickers y documentos. Entrá a los grupos más activos y elimina archivos pesados o innecesarios.
- Desactivar (o limitar) la descarga automática.
En los ajustes de WhatsApp, revisá la configuración de descarga automática y desactivala para los tipos de archivo que no necesitas guardar (por ejemplo, videos o documentos). Esto evita que se acumulen sin que lo notes.
PUBLICIDAD
- Controlar los respaldos automáticos.
Las copias de seguridad de conversaciones pueden incluir archivos multimedia y ocupar espacio tanto en el teléfono como en la nube. Revisa la configuración de backups para evitar que crezcan de forma sostenida.
- Hacer una limpieza más amplia del teléfono.
Si el problema es general de almacenamiento, también ayuda: borrar aplicaciones que no usas, eliminar duplicados o contenido repetido en la galería y mover fotos y videos a servicios en la nube (por ejemplo, Google Fotos o iCloud).
PUBLICIDAD
- Vaciar la caché de aplicaciones.
Con el uso, las apps acumulan datos temporales que pueden ocupar varios gigabytes; limpiar la caché puede liberar espacio.
Qué nuevas funciones hay en WhatsApp
WhatsApp sumó en los últimos meses una serie de funciones pensadas para usar la app con más comodidad en distintos dispositivos y, a la vez, ordenar mejor las conversaciones.
PUBLICIDAD
Entre las novedades, se destaca la posibilidad de registrar una cuenta directamente desde iPad, sin necesidad de vincularla previamente con un teléfono, una mejora clave para quienes ya usan la tablet como pantalla principal para trabajar o estudiar.
También hubo un rediseño de la experiencia en el auto: la app actualizó su integración con Apple CarPlay y Android Auto para escuchar y responder mensajes, hacer llamadas, ver el historial y acceder a favoritos con manos libres desde la pantalla del vehículo.
PUBLICIDAD
En los chats, la plataforma amplió herramientas para tomar decisiones y coordinar grupos.
Las encuestas ahora permiten fijar un horario de cierre, ocultar los nombres de quienes votan y editar la pregunta dentro de los 15 minutos posteriores a su publicación.
PUBLICIDAD
Además, llegó @all, una mención para avisar a todos sobre mensajes urgentes, con la opción de silenciar ese tipo de notificación. También se incorporó una forma más simple de crear un nuevo grupo a partir de uno existente, sin volver a agregar contactos uno por uno.
En llamadas, WhatsApp habilitó audio y videollamadas desde el navegador (WhatsApp Web), tanto individuales como grupales, sin descargar una app adicional, y con funciones como compartir pantalla, reacciones y una pestaña de llamadas con historial y favoritos.
PUBLICIDAD
Sumó, además, transferencia de llamadas entre dispositivos, sala de espera en enlaces con aprobación, QuickHD para iniciar en alta definición y supresión de ruido para mejorar el audio en entornos ruidosos.
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: Photoroom proved a one-click wonder for making product shots unmissable
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Photoroom mostly does what it says: transform photos of your products into something that looks professional and enticing. The tools are easy to use, and in the main they work really well. If you have an online retail business, this platform gives your products that professional look you were after.
Pros
- +Most AI tools work amazingly well
- +Easy to use
- +Works on many browsers
- +Supports HEIC image format
Cons
- -AI Credits can run out fast
- -Sometimes need to repeat your request for it to work
- -Video Generator needs some work
Why you can trust TechRadar
I've been intrigued by AI photo editors for a while now. Some work well, some not so well. Photoroom falls into the former camp. By and large, I found the AI tools to be very impressive and intuitive to use. There are some caveats to that which I'll get into, but overall, Photoroom delivered what it promises.
But what does it promise, exactly? Now, compared to a lot of AI photo editors, things here are a little different. This isn't a platform for touching up your holiday snaps or brightening up social media posts.
The emphasis here is on business use. Effectively, if you run an online store or similar, then you use Photoroom to transform staid, dull product shots into more enticing and engaging imagery that pops off the page.
Keen to see how it's developed since we last reviewed it three years ago - AI has come a long way since then - I tried out the platform to see what I could create.
Photoroom: Pricing & plans
- Online service via browser, iOS and Android app
- Aimed at businesses large and small
- Reasonably priced subscriptions and free trial
You can check out Photoroom by clicking here.
The platform is available online through a dedicated app for your iPhone or Android phone, or if you’re working on a computer, via your favourite web browser. Unlike many I've tested, you're not restricted to either Chrome or Edge here.
As with any online service, you need to subscribe to it to use it with a monthly cost billed annually. Photoroom comes in three tiers.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
‘Pro', recommended for ‘solopreneurs’, will cost you $13 per month, billed annually. This level grants you 4,250 AI credits monthly, allows you to perform 1,000 exports, and comes with Photoroom’s standard set of tools.
The middle tier is ‘Max’ and is designed for small businesses. For $35 a month (again, billed annually - all tiers are), your credits are upped to 12,000, your exports to 3,000, and the advanced ‘Video Generator’ tool is now available.
Finally, there’s 'Ultra', for “growing brands”. You’re given 20,000 AI credits,10,000 exports, and can create videos and images in 4K, all for $100 a month.
If you’re looking for a more bespoke option, there’s a tailor-made Enterprise tier, with a tailor-made cost to match.
I recommend checking prices as Photoroom often offer discounts on those standard prices. Plus, you can try any of these tiers free for seven days, although don’t forget to cancel your trial before that should you decide not to carry on with the service and you’re needlessly charged a hefty sum for your forgetfulness.
Photoroom was generous enough to grant me access to their Ultra tier, so let’s see what it’s capable of, and what you can do with all those AI credits.
- Pricing & plans: 4 / 5
Photoroom: Interface
- Simple, well designed, and clear interface
- Easy ways to import images and work on them
- For an online service, I was impressed
The interface is simple and well organised. Once you’ve logged in to your account, you’ll find a sidebar to the left which contains various tools you need.
Thiss includes all the AI tools in your arsenal, templates, a direct link to your Shopify account if you have one, a batch tool so you can work on up to 250 images at once, a Brand Kit where you keep all your assets, and a Design section where your products’ photos are stored.
All the AI tools, which are essentially all your editing tools, are easy to use: you select one, upload a new photo or select one already in your account, apply the effect and you’re done.
There is one thing that I found surprising: Photoroom supports HEIC, the High Efficiency Image Container. It’s a highly compressed image format that’s been around since 2015 and has been increasingly prevalent since Apple made it the default image format for their iPhones in 2017.
The reason I make a point of mentioning this is because far too many services still do not support it, forcing any image or photo saved as an HEIC to be converted into either a JPEG or PNG prior to import. There is no such issue here, saving you time and frustration.
- Interface: 4.5 / 5
Photoroom: Tools
- On the whole, the AI tools do an absolutely excellent job
- Impressive ways to transform passable shots into something potential customers will love
- But... not all tools are created equal
Such a service succeeds on the strength of its tools, and Photoroom iss betting the farm on AI for this. But AI is a very generic term these days. Is it really artificial intelligence to remove an image’s background?
I’d put it more in the “complex algorithm does a very good job with what it’s given” category. Same with removing objects or people from a photograph and replacing it with an artificially generated background that blends with the existing one.
Such tools already existed before “AI” became an all-encompassing marketing brand. Or, taking inspiration from Monty Python's The Life of Brian, “it’s not AI, it’s a very clever tool”.
But whether it’s AI or not is less important than how these tools fare: I found the achieved results to be excellent. More often than not in apps like Photoshop or Pixelmator Pro, I end up having to touch up the output of similar tools, but here, it was essentially a one-click wonder.
Tools that really impressed me were definitely more AI based. Say you want to sell a shirt, which you’ve photographed on a surface, with as few wrinkles as you can manage… except you know how it is: such layouts are never really good enough.
Well fret no more: Photoroom has a tool that digitally irons your shirt for you, transforming your amateurish-looking photo into a meticulously smooth out product. Couple that with the background remover tool, and you’re well on your way to have a professional looking photograph.
But why stop there? Photoroom has a bunch of AI-generated models who can wear your outfit for you. There’s even what they call a ‘ghost mannequin’ to puff up your shirt so customers can see what it would look like on someone, without being distracted by an actual (or virtual) person wearing it.
I found all this pretty incredible, and that’s just scratching the surface. It’s not all sunshine and rainbows though: for instance, Photoroom has a Video Generator.
Select a photo, browse through all available templates, maybe even type in a prompt if you need, and the AI will get to work… this is where I encountered the familiar “AI tries way too hard yet fails miserably” syndrome.
Some templates removed my test products from the usual confines of physical reality, sometimes in a most disturbing way. Or they just didn’t work at all as expected. I trust the team working hard on this aspect of the service (what I was able to use bore no relation to their intro video about it, so things are moving fast in this arena), but for now, maybe stick with still images, where the results are truly impressive.
Photoroom: AI credits
- Set number of monthly credits, so use them wisely
- Many common AI tools don't cost any credits at all
- However, sometimes, the requested action won’t work, so try, try again
As you’d expect, most AI tools will cost you credits. A video generation goes for 500 (money not well spent for now), Exporting an image at 2K or 4K will cost you 135 and 240 credits respectively, adding an AI background to an image is worth 5 credits, and so forth.
Thankfully though, some tools you’ll use most often, like removing the background of a shot, retouching a photo or performing some image enhancements won’t cost you a thing (beyond your subscription).
You’ll just have to balance what you are given each month with what you hope to achieve in that time period, with the relief that when an action doesn’t work, you won’t have lost any credits - yes, sometimes an error occurs.
However, I found that if I request the same action again - and again - it finally does what I asked it to. Teething problems, I’m sure, and at least it does work impressively well eventually.
Should I buy Photoroom?
Buy it if...
You’re looking to sell a ton of product and want the images advertising your wares to look their best, using a service that is well designed, and is easy to use (when it works)
Don't buy it if...
You don’t want to encourage the proliferation of AI, know your way around Photoshop anyway, and can’t justify yet another subscription, no matter how great some effects are.
How I tested Photoroom
I tested this service on my trusty Apple MacBook Pro. Generally I do my best to check how software works on a variety of devices, both Macs and PCs and portable devices, when needed.
But as this was an online service, whose tools are dependent on servers the main bottleneck would be my fibre connection. I experienced no issues on that score.
Everything was extremely responsive. The free tools were nearly instantaneous, and depending on the complexity of what I was asking the AI to do, it took gradually longer.
Video creation took the longest amount of time, clocking in at around 4 minutes for me. Still, that didn't feel like a long time, when I got it working.
For more creative tools, we tested the best photo editors.
Steve has been writing about technology since 2003. Starting with Digital Creative Arts, he's since added his tech expertise at titles such as iCreate, MacFormat, MacWorld, MacLife, and TechRadar. His focus is on the creative arts, like website builders, image manipulation, and filmmaking software, but he hasn’t shied away from more business-oriented software either. He uses many of the apps he writes about in his personal and professional life. Steve loves how computers have enabled everyone to delve into creative possibilities, and is always delighted to share his knowledge, expertise, and experience with readers.

articles.title: Apple declara obsoletos estos modelos de iPhone y Macbook
articles.text:
Apple ha declarado obsoletos al iPhone X y al MacBook Pro de 15 pulgadas de 2018, dejando sin soporte oficial de hardware y reparaciones a ambos dispositivos. Esta actualización en la lista de productos de la compañía marca el fin del servicio para dos modelos que fueron fundamentales en la evolución de su catálogo.
Cuando un producto pasa a la categoría de “obsoleto”, Apple y sus proveedores de servicio autorizados dejan de ofrecer cualquier tipo de reparación o recambio, sin importar si el dispositivo continúa en garantía. Antes de alcanzar este estado, los dispositivos permanecen un tiempo en la lista “vintage”, durante el cual aún pueden recibir servicio siempre que existan piezas disponibles.
PUBLICIDAD
Generalmente, Apple considera obsoleto un producto cuando ya han transcurrido más de siete años desde que dejó de comercializarlo.
Esta nueva clasificación afecta especialmente a quienes dependen de estos equipos, ya que una falla en el hardware, como una batería desgastada o una pantalla dañada, solo podrá solucionarse fuera de los canales oficiales y sin garantía de disponibilidad de piezas originales.
PUBLICIDAD
El iPhone X, un punto de inflexión en la gama
El iPhone X se lanzó en noviembre de 2017 y se retiró del mercado en septiembre de 2018. Fue el primer modelo de la marca en incorporar una pantalla OLED de borde a borde y la tecnología Face ID, eliminando el botón físico de inicio. Este dispositivo también introdujo el diseño de parte trasera de cristal y el marco de acero inoxidable, que se mantuvieron en generaciones posteriores del iPhone.
Durante su vida útil, el iPhone X recibió actualizaciones hasta iOS 16 y nunca fue compatible con iOS 17. Actualmente, su última versión disponible es iOS 16.7.16. Aunque el teléfono sigue funcionando, la falta de soporte para nuevas actualizaciones y la imposibilidad de obtener reparaciones oficiales limitan su vida útil en el ecosistema de la marca.
PUBLICIDAD
El MacBook Pro de 15 pulgadas de 2018 y el teclado butterfly
El MacBook Pro de 15 pulgadas de 2018 llegó al mercado en julio de ese año e incorporó por primera vez el chip de seguridad T2. El equipo también es recordado por incluir el teclado butterfly, un diseño criticado por su baja fiabilidad. Apple mantuvo un programa de reparación específico para estos teclados hasta 2024.
Este MacBook Pro puede ejecutar macOS Sequoia, pero no recibirá versiones posteriores. La última versión disponible es macOS 15.7.7, lo que supone un límite claro para quienes buscan mantener actualizado el sistema operativo en sus dispositivos.
PUBLICIDAD
¿Qué ocurre tras la declaración de obsolescencia?
Ser declarado obsoleto no implica que el dispositivo deje de funcionar. Tanto el iPhone X como el MacBook Pro de 2018 seguirán operativos, pero cualquier avería requerirá acudir a servicios no oficiales o buscar piezas de terceros, cuya disponibilidad no está asegurada. En algunos casos, Apple puede extender el acceso a piezas hasta una década, aunque la empresa no garantiza este plazo para todos los modelos ni en todas las regiones.
Para quienes todavía dependen de estos equipos, no existe una urgencia inmediata por reemplazarlos solo por el cambio de clasificación, pero sí se recomienda anticipar posibles necesidades de reparación. Si la batería muestra signos de desgaste o el teclado falla, es probable que resulte más difícil encontrar soluciones a través de los canales tradicionales de la compañía.
PUBLICIDAD
Quienes aún utilicen un iPhone X pueden considerar actualizarse a la serie iPhone 17 o esperar el lanzamiento de la próxima línea iPhone 18. En el caso de los usuarios del MacBook Pro de 2018, la decisión dependerá del estado actual del equipo y de la necesidad de contar con soporte oficial ante eventuales problemas de hardware.
El cambio en la política de soporte refuerza la importancia de planificar la renovación de dispositivos y anticipar la transición a modelos más recientes dentro del ecosistema de Apple.

articles.title: Fans aren't just for summer — here are 5 alternative uses for your personal cooler, from styling hair to drying socks
articles.text:
From styling your hair to drying your socks — 5 ways to use your portable fan in between heatwaves
A handheld electric fan makes a huge difference during summer heatwaves, but there's no need to stash it away in a drawer when the weather cools down. Whether you need an ad-hoc hair styler or a quick way to cool your kids' dinner without blowing on it, your mini fan can be your best friend.
Great fans don't have to be expensive, either. I recently tested five portable fans from across the price spectrum, and the most expensive model was outranked by a humble model costing a fifth of the price.
1. Drying your hair
When reviewing the Dyson HushJet Mini Cool Fan, I noted that "even on the lowest setting, you can really feel it; dial it up to maximum and it’s as powerful as some hairdryers I’ve used" — and it seems some fan-owners follow that thought to its natural conclusion, using their portable coolers to help dry and style their locks without heat — though it might not yield particularly sleek results.
"Drying my hair on electric fan sounds less damaging than blow drying it," said one user in Reddit's haircare community. "My genuine question is: does it contribute to the frizziness of my hair?"
According to experts, cool air from a fan might do exactly that. We recently interviewed Dr Julie Chung, CEO and founder of haircare brand T3, who suggested that heat styling can be a better choice for the health of your hair.
"Heat in general has been sort of demonized incorrectly," she tells told us. "Women always think, 'Oh heat is terrible for my hair, I'm just gonna let it air dry, I'm gonna shower and just sleep on it.' Hair is actually in its most fragile state when it's wet. It tends to be much easier to break — that tensile strength is decreased and it's more likely to snap.
"And not to mention when you air-dry your hair, usually the hair is very frizzy and it tends to look even unhealthier if your hair is already in a dried out state."
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
2. Drying laundry
Portable fans are particularly popular in Singapore, where the hot and humid summers make them a necessity for daily life, so it's no surprise that members of the Ask Singapore community on Reddit have some particularly creative ideas.
One inventive traveler explained that they use their portable fan to dry small items of laundry, which could be a helpful hack when you're on a long vacation and don't have enough socks to last the whole trip.
Just don't try washing your underwear in the hotel coffee machine. The bathroom sink will do just fine.
3. Drying nail polish
You can buy electric fans specifically designed for drying nail polish, which can cost up to $70 / £50 / AU$100, so it makes sense to save your cash that instead to finish your manicure in record time.
"Whether you're at a salon or home, cold air from a fan or blow dryer will help the polish harden faster," Sarah Gibson Tuttle, founder of nail products company Olive & June, told beauty site Byrdie in an interview.
However, opinion seems to be divided on whether this actually helps, or if it's more likely to spoil the finish of your polish.
"[Many] people use fans or blow dryers to speed up the drying process, and while it works by evaporating the solvents faster, you can run into bubbles forming in the polish," said professional nail artist Amy Oung.
Perhaps give it a try and see what you think. Of course, this will only work on regular nail polish — gel polish needs to be cured with a UV light.
4. Cooling hot food
Many handheld fans have stands or folding stems that allow them to double as desk fans, which can be a handy tool for parents.
"My handheld fan can prop on the table," one parent said. "Very useful for when the food is too hot for my kid to eat but [I'm too lazy to] blow. I just blast the fan at it for few seconds."
Not as cute as the cat-shaped drink-cooling robot Nékojita FuFu, which we saw at last year's IFA show in Berlin, perhaps, but certainly more affordable.
5. Fidgeting
Fans aren't just for purely practical purposes — they can also provide something to occupy restless hands. One fan-owning Singaporean Redditor said they originally "Bought it for survival, kept it for emotional support."
"I use it waiting for buses, walking between MRT exits, in crowded lifts, and weirdly… when I’m anxious or bored," they explained. "It’s basically a socially acceptable fidget spinner at this point."
Do you use your fan for something other than keeping cool and comfortable? Let us know using the poll below, or in the comments.

articles.title: ‘Smoother than an olympic diver slathered in goose fat’ — the affordable OnePlus Nord CE5 seriously impressed me with its slick performance and fluid 120Hz display
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Given its affordable price, using the OnePlus Nord CE5 is a surprisingly polished experience. Both its display and camera deliver seriously dynamic color, its OS is smooth to use and makes multitasking a breeze, and its battery can outlast many flagship phones. Admittedly, its chipset is far from top of the range, it’s packed with more bloat than I’d like, and it can’t handle games on max graphics settings, but none of its shortcomings are egregious. It’s a seriously skilled phone in many areas given its low price tag.
Pros
- +Vibrant display
- +Great productivity performance and gesture control
- +Rich, colorful photography
- +Epic 20-hour battery life
Cons
- -Middling chipset
- -Too much bloat
- -Limited to 2x optical zoom
Why you can trust TechRadar
OnePlus Nord CE5 review: two-minute review
The OnePlus Nord CE5 is an affordable yet premium-feeling handset that punches way above its weight. Although its successor, the CE6, has launched in some markets, OnePlus has confirmed that it and future handsets will no longer sell in the UK. So, in lieu of a newer version, is the CE5 still worth your consideration?
The OnePlus Nord CE5’s design certainly doesn’t make it look bargain basement, but it doesn’t feel super luxe either. While it’s pleasantly tactile under your fingertips, there’s no confusing its plastic edges for metal, and I’m not totally bowled over by the pearlescent effect on the Marble Mist colorway. However, I will grant that it feels solidly made and its vertical camera module looks pretty neat when so many handsets’ lenses look like they’ve been grafted on by Dr. Frankenstein.
Although it’s not a total knockout, the Nord CE5’s display definitely packs a punch given its price. Colors are bold and vivid, making the nature documentaries I was watching seriously pop. Its 387PPI display showed off most images in crisp detail, even if it wasn’t as pin sharp as some of the best phones. On the flip side, whites run a little bit blue for my liking, and the display is not quite bright enough to make up for how reflective its screen is. Still, there was plenty about the screen that dazzled me, figuratively at least.
Under the hood, the Nord CE5 runs the MediaTek Dimensity 8350 Apex chipset. That’s not a current-gen SoC by any means, but I still got great productivity performance out of it. Not only was I able to have myriad apps open, but I also ran Google Docs and a streaming app in split-screen with no noticeable slowdown.
Gaming performance was also pretty stable. Playing lengthy sessions of both Call of Duty: Mobile and Genshin Impact, the Nord CE5 ran very smoothly and showed no hint of lag or jitter. Cranking the graphics settings up to their highest on Genshin Impact did throw up a warning that I was overclocking the CPU, though, so while performance remained stable, you might not want to run things that high. On the plus side, the Nord CE5 didn’t experience all that much warming during this, thanks to its CryoVelocity graphene vapor chamber.
Based on Android 15, the OxygenOS 15.0 that the Nord CE5 runs on is nice and agile. Multitasking is easy thanks to its split-screen mode and there are great shortcuts on offer, like screen-off gestures that let you open the camera or switch on the flashlight by tracing an O or V on the display. On the whole, its AI tools are unobtrusive yet helpful, and OnePlus offers a full six years of software updates. The only thing I don’t love here is the bloat that comes pre-installed — seriously, phone makers, can you stop foisting Temu on me?
For a phone in this price range, the Nord CE5 also offers a very decent camera. Whether I was popping off shots of brilliant yellow roses or the deep blue sky reflected in a river, colors felt vibrant and its HDR performance rendered textures like stonework with a nice depth. Admittedly, its smaller 1/1.95 inch sensor can’t quite rival flagship phones in terms of sheer detail, but it still captured textures and details with real precision. And even though I’d personally prefer at least a 3x lens in my camera, the 2x zoom conveyed excellent detail without showing any distortions or aberrations.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
In my book, though, by far the Nord CE5’s strongest feature is its battery. OnePlus has managed to eke more than 20 hours of life out of its 5,200mAh battery, meaning it can happily outlast many of the flagship phones we’ve reviewed in recent times. Not only that, but during my testing I found its 80W SUPERVOOC charging could comfortably juice it up from 0% to 100% in just 59 minutes, which is blisteringly fast.
All in all, the Nord CE5 is a solid, if unexceptional, phone… until you consider its price point. Considering a list price that starts at £299, there are many areas it pulls ahead of similarly priced rivals, while in some areas — chiefly battery life — it can honestly give flagships a run for their money. Ultimately, if your intended spend sits on the border between budget and mid-range phone, the Nord CE5 has plenty of highlights and few enough deficits to make it a worthy investment.
OnePlus Nord CE5 review: Specs
| Dimensions | 6.44 x 2.99 x 0.32 inches / 163.6 x 76.0 x 8.2mm | 
| Weight | 199g | 
| Screen | 6.77-inch Fluid AMOLED | 
| Resolution | 2392 x 1080 pixels (FHD+, ~387 ppi) | 
| Refresh rate | 120Hz | 
| Chipset | MediaTek Dimensity 8350 Apex | 
| RAM | 8GB / 12GB (LPDDR5X) | 
| Storage | 128GB / 256GB (UFS 3.1, expandable via MicroSD up to 1TB) | 
| OS | OxygenOS 15.0 based on Android 15 | 
| Rear cameras | 50 MP main (f/1.8, OIS, Sony LYT-600) + 8 MP ultra-wide (f/2.2, 112° FOV) | 
| Front camera | 16 MP (f/2.4) | 
| Battery | 5,200mAh | 
| Charging | 80W SUPERVOOC wired | 
OnePlus Nord CE5 review: Price and availability
- Launched on July 8, 2025
- List price of £299 for 128GB storage or £349 for 256GB
- Succeeded by the Nord CE6 — but that’s not available in the UK
Having launched on July 8, 2025, the OnePlus Nord CE5 is currently available in the UK. While it has technically been supplanted by the OnePlus Nord CE6, released on May 8, 2026, the latter isn't sold in the UK and, with no launch rumored, is unlikely to make it here at all. So that means the Nord CE5 is still the budget OnePlus to aim for if you’re a Brit.
When it comes to cost, the Nord CE5 retails for a list price of £299 for the model with 128GB of storage or £349 for 256GB. That means it leans slightly more toward budget territory than mid-range. You can choose from one of two colorways for that spend, either the minimal Black Infinity version or the iridescent Marble Mist I’ve tested here.
OnePlus Nord CE5 review: design
- Solid, robust-feeling design
- Easy to hold one-handed
- Personally not keen on marble colorway
Overall, I like the build of the OnePlus Nord CE5. While it doesn’t quite feel as premium as more expensive phones — that lightweight plastic trim around its edge can’t compete with my iPhone 16 Pro’s titanium, for example — that flat design still feels comfortable in your hand.
Measuring 6.44 x 2.99 inches / 163.58 x 76.02mm, the Nord CE5 is slightly taller and less broad than some of its affordable rivals, making it easy to hold in one hand — although you might need your second hand to reach the very top of the screen. But, at 0.33 inches / 8.27mm, and 0.32 inches / 8.17mm deep for the Marble Mist / Black Infinity versions respectively, it’s not the thinnest device on the market, with only a few handsets like the Nothing Phone (4a), iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max being thicker.
As I’ve mentioned above, the Nord CE5 comes in two colorways: Black Infinity and Marble Mist. Honestly, I’m not a huge fan of the pearlescent marble effect — while it sounds premium, in reality it looks a touch gaudy to me. On the plus side, its matte finish feels wonderfully smooth, with just enough of a grain to remain tactile.
Perhaps unsurprisingly given the budget price, its design is pretty minimal elsewhere. But that’s actually something of a relief, given how crowded some flagship phones can now feel with their full-width camera modules and bunches of bonus buttons. The Nord CE5’s vertically aligned dual-lens camera module looks neat and nicely self-contained, while it only has a lock button and volume rocker adorning one edge, making it feel lean and sparing.
- Design score: 3.5 / 5
OnePlus Nord CE5 review: display
- Vibrant, satisfying colors
- Solid resolution, albeit not flagship sharp
- Lacking in brightness
Measuring 6.77 inches, the OnePlus Nord CE5’s screen is more expansive than that of many flagships. It outstrips the iPhone 17 Pro and Samsung Galaxy 26+ at 6.3 and 6.7 inches respectively, although it’s not quite as extensive as phones like the 6.83-inch Nothing Phone (4a) Pro or the 6.9-inch iPhone 17 Pro Max and Samsung Galaxy 26 Ultra.
OnePlus has shared 2392 x 1080 pixels across that display, giving the Nord CE5 a pixel density of 387PPI. Keen to see how that stacks up in practice, I streamed Planet Earth II in 1080p on the Nord CE5 side-by-side with my 460PPI iPhone 16 Pro. During a scene involving a pride of lionesses on the savannah grappling with an African buffalo, the Nord CE5 felt just a tiny bit less crisp, with the drops and spray of water being cast up not feeling quite as sharp as on my premium phone. Most images still look pretty crisp though, even if they’re not quite up to flagship standard.
On paper, the OnePlus Nord CE5 offers 1430 nits peak brightness and a typical brightness of 800 nits. Unfortunately, its display didn’t exactly feel dazzlingly bright to me. Some scenes felt like their white level was a bit too low; for example, the canopy of a jungle looked thicker and more oppressive than it did on other screens. And the whites that are there are a little too cold for my liking, with the white highlights of exposed tree bark looking a little on the blue side.
This isn’t helped by the fact that the Nord CE5’s display is quite reflective. While most phones reflect the lighting in the TechRadar testing labs — they're huge fluorescent ceiling panels — the OnePlus’s display seems to mirror many other objects in the room as well. Without the extra brightness that more expensive models are capable of, it can’t quite overcome local sources of light.
That’s a shame because the Nord CE5’s color fidelity is pretty spot on elsewhere. Watching a Wilson’s bird of paradise trying to court a mate, I was impressed with how vibrantly the display rendered its bright blue crown, red back and yellow mantle, not to mention its bright green fluorescent collar. But thanks to that slight paucity of white highlights, it still doesn’t have quite the HDR pop it otherwise could have.
I’ll give the Nord CE5 credit where it’s due though: the display’s max 120Hz refresh rate ensures that everything looks smoother than an Olympic diver slathered in goose fat. Navigating menus and swiping between apps, everything felt wonderfully fluid and never showed even a hint of judder or slowdown. The device can absolutely rival any premium handset here.
- Display score: 3.5 / 5
OnePlus Nord CE5 review: Software
- Great gestures and shortcuts built in
- Unobtrusive AI tools
- Quite a lot of bloat
Running OxygenOS 15.0, based on Android 15, the OnePlus Nord CE5 offers a pretty clean software experience with some seriously clever shortcuts built in. I like being able to swipe down with three fingers to take screenshots, while screen-off gestures that allow you to open the camera by tracing an O or switch on the flashlight by tracing a V are a fun touch. I can also see being able to lift the phone to my ear to auto-answer calls or flip it screen-down to mute them as features I’d end up using a lot.
On top of this, the Nord CE5 offers solid productivity features. For example, the smart sidebar allows you to quickly access your most-used apps by swiping from the top-right of the screen. Split View allows you to drag and drop two windows into a split-screen mode — not only does this feel super fluid to do, but you can easily resize each window by dragging the boundary between them.
It’s a little unfortunate then that OnePlus doesn’t seem able to resist the temptation to burden this otherwise lightweight experience with unnecessary bloat. Don’t get me wrong: it’s not the worst offender in this category. But the Nord CE5 still includes loads of apps that really should not be included by default, like AliExpress, Amazon Music or TikTok. Honestly, phone manufacturers: stop doing this.
The AI features on the Nord CE5 certainly aren’t as extreme as a phone like the Honor 600, with its Image to Video and wild VFX tools, but there are some useful tools available for tweaking your photos. Not only can you remove blur and reflections and upscale the quality of your images, but you can also erase those annoying people who walk straight through your shot and swap in a different expression for that one friend who always seems to have their eyes closed.
Overall, AI features are nicely unobtrusive, which is good news for those who are more AI-agnostic. The Google Gemini app comes pre-installed, offering answers, generative text and images. But if you’re not interested in its help, it’s easy to remove from your home and lockscreen, a pleasingly light-touch approach compared to some of the more gung-ho handsets.
Even if it doesn’t have the most cutting-edge advances, you can be sure the Nord CE5 will last you for the long haul. That’s because OnePlus has committed to providing six years of software support for its handset, something that’s definitely appreciated in an era when more of us are trying to eke more longevity out of our handsets, rather than ditch them every year.
All told, the software the Nord CE5 offers here isn’t groundbreaking. But it’s smooth and super-usable. Just please, OnePlus: shed some of that bloat.
- Software score: 4 / 5
OnePlus Nord CE5 review: performance
- Not the highest power chipset
- But productivity and gaming largely ran smoothly
- Very capable cooling
Given the OnePlus Nord CE5’s affordable price point, you won’t be surprised to hear that it doesn’t pack a top-of-the-range chipset. Don’t get me wrong: its MediaTek Dimensity 8350 Apex SoC isn’t bad, offering roughly similar performance to something like the Snapdragon 7 Gen 4, but it doesn't offer as much thrust as many current flagship chips. With 8GB of RAM backing this up, I was expecting decent if unexceptional performance here.
And that’s generally what I found. During day-to-day productivity use, the Nord CE5 seems to run smoothly. Dipping in and out of apps, I never found any delays or witnessed anything hanging, no matter how many I opened. I even tried typing part of this review in split-screen mode while streaming What We Do In The Shadows — admittedly, this was atrocious for helping me focus, but both Google Docs and the video were unfaltering, marching on without a single misstep.
The Nord CE5 has surprisingly good gaming performance, given its budget price too. Playing Call of Duty: Mobile with the high-res texture packs, everything ran smoother than cappuccino foam. I played around eight ranked matches back-to-back and at no point did any judder or lag cause me to lose my kill-streak or stop me hoovering up MVP awards.
Genshin Impact was warier of the MediaTek Dimensity 8350 Apex chipset. While I was able to get balanced performance on the Higher graphics setting, switching it up to the Highest setting gave me a warning that I was overclocking the chipset. Despite this, the game still ran without any real issues — it’s possible the game developers were being overcautious, but I’ve obviously not conducted any long-term testing on how this might affect the life of the chip, so I’d urge caution before doing the same.
While some mid-range processors I’ve tested lately have gotten pretty warm during extended play sessions, I’m pleased to say that’s not an issue here. Thanks to its CryoVelocity graphene vapor chamber with a 7041mm² cooling area, the Nord CE5 stayed frosty even with Genshin Impact running at its overclocked settings. So while you might not get flagship-level performance out of the Nord CE5, it packs a pretty decent punch for such a low cost.
- Performance score: 4 / 5

OnePlus Nord CE5 review: camera
- Lush, vibrant colors
- Pro camera mode built-in
- Only offers 2x optical zoom
For the price, I was expecting the OnePlus Nord CE5’s camera to feel limited, but it’s actually relatively talented. First off, it’s capable of some bold, punchy HDR. One shot I snapped nearing the golden hour of a stone urn on a pedestal showed really deep blacks, while the highlights were warm enough to feel true-to-life.
Thanks to its 50MP resolution main lens, the OnePlus Nord CE5 is capable of crisp resolution, although its 1/1.95 inch sensor can't keep up with those offered by flagships. Zooming into a shot I took of a bumblebee crawling over a thistle, its detail was pleasingly crisp and kept everything wonderfully sharp. But, by comparison, my iPhone 16 Pro picked up every speck of pollen on its fuzzy coat in sharp detail and captured the sun reflected in its glossy black eye.
Colors are also captured with a real vibrance, the petals of a rose rendered in a wonderfully rich pink, for example. Naturally, you can’t expect top-tier chromatic performance here — my iPhone conveyed more range between darker and lighter tones and gave the dappling of each petal more pop. But the Nord CE5 still records delightfully lush hues and at least avoids the shortcut some brands take of oversaturating certain shades to artificially make images seem more vivid.
When taking photos close up, the OnePlus has a much shallower depth of field compared to some phones I’ve used. While that’s useful for creating a wonderful depth effect in your images, it does mean the Nord CE5 sometimes struggles to keep the whole subject in focus — some of the petals of a purple coneflower I shot looked slightly less crisp than on my iPhone, for example. Having said that, I actually quite like its bokeh, which feels much more Gaussian and subtle compared to phones that tend to make their bokeh too sharp and ‘swirly’.
While there are some decent Pro camera apps out there that unlock more granular control over your phone’s snapper, I love that OnePlus has already parceled this up in the Nord CE5’s native camera app. Using the Pro setting, I was able to tweak the camera’s ISO and shutter speed, as well as its white balance. For me though, the most invaluable setting is the manual lens’s focus, although this is far harder to set accurately on a phone screen than a DSLR viewfinder, so I do wish OnePlus had created a shortcut for zooming in on the screen while tweaking the focal range.
Night photography on the Nord CE5 is also generally strong. Taking shots at my favorite riverside pub at dusk, it struck a good balance between light and dark, with bright highlights not feeling overblown without compromising the shadows. Occasionally, faces could look a little soft around the edges, but that may have just been my subject not remaining as still as they could have. And at least the phone avoids overexposing night-time images — I’m not Truffaut, so I have no desire to shoot day for night or vice versa.
One area where I’d say the Nord CE5 falls further short of more premium phones is the zoom lenses. While the phone has a decent 2x optical zoom, it did make me realize how dependent I’ve become on my phone’s 5x optical zoom. On the plus side, the Nord CE5’s zoom lenses are crisp and distortion-free — the shots I snapped of flapping sky rats pigeons near a local river rendered their wings in decent detail.
All things considered, the Nord CE5’s camera is very good. Not only is using it an uncluttered experience, but its shots feel a lot truer to life than some of the flashier cams on other mid-market phones.
- Camera score: 4 / 5
OnePlus Nord CE5 review: battery
- Lengthy 20-hour battery life
- 80W charging fills battery in an hour
OnePlus generally packages outstanding batteries with its handsets, and the Nord CE5 is no exception. The brand suggests you should get several days of normal usage out of the CE5’s 5200mAh battery before needing to charge it.
Eager to put these claims to the test, I set the phone to stream a 2K video at 50% brightness on a loop — after 6 hours it had dropped to 71%, so I’d expect it to last roughly 20 hours and 40 minutes total. Not only does that mean OnePlus’s estimates are pretty on the money, but it also means the Nord CE5 comfortably outlasts many of the best phones on the market, whether premium options like the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra or budget bangers like Google Pixel 10a.
But where the OnePlus Nord CE5 really leaves all competition eating its dust is charging. Thanks to OnePlus’s 80W SUPERVOOC charging, topping up this handset feels faster than a pitstop fuel change — hooking it up to a cable and brick rated for up to 100W, it took around 59 minutes to go from 0% to 100%. While that’s not quite as ludicrous as the OnePlus 15’s blistering 120W charging, it still means you could juice it back up in the time it took you to scarf down your lunchtime bagel and boba tea.
So if your biggest priority in a budget phone is that it can last alongside you on your busiest days, the OnePlus Nord CE5 has definitely got you covered.
- Battery score: 5 / 5
Should I buy the OnePlus Nord CE5?
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Design | Solid, well-built design, narrow aspect ratio makes it easy to grasp in the hand. Not the biggest fan of the faux marble colorway though. | 3.5 / 5 | 
| Display | Expansive 6.77-inch display, rich colors, super-smooth 120Hz refresh rate, strong resolution even if it falls a little short of flagships, 1430-nit peak didn’t feel that bright, especially given how reflective the screen could be. | 3.5 / 5 | 
| Software | Smooth agile OS, great screen-off gestures and raise-to-answer functionality, solid productivity tools, discreet AI tools, six years of software support, annoying unnecessary bloatware. | 4 / 5 | 
| Performance | Chipset not top of the range but fares well, never witnessed any lag during productivity tasks and split-screening, games ran smoothly although running the highest graphics settings forced me to overclock the SoC, stayed cool during heavy loads. | 4 / 5 | 
| Cameras | Striking hues, strong contrast, good resolution that falls just a little short of flagships, surprisingly good low-light performance, soft subtle bokeh, only offers up to a 2x zoom. | 4 / 5 | 
| Battery life | Lengthy 20-hour battery, can charge from 0% to 100% in just 59 minutes. | 5 / 5 | 
| Value | While the Nord CE5 isn’t perfect, it offers quality that rivals many mid-market phones. And when you factor in its starting price of £299, that’s a whole heap of quality for not much cash. | 5 / 5 | 
Buy it if…
You need a battery that will go the distance
If you never want to get blindsided by an empty battery, the Nord CE5 has you covered. Not only should its 5,200mAh battery last you around 20 hours, but you can fully charge it in just one hour via its 80W SUPERVOOC.
You want a solid camera for a cheap price
Having tested a few mid-range phones whose cameras cut corners or overprocessed images, the Nord CE5’s camera is a breath of fresh air, focusing on getting the fundamentals right.
Don’t buy it if…
You’re after a top-tier gaming phone
If you like some casual gaming, the Nord CE5 will still deliver rock-solid stability. But if you want to play on the highest graphic settings, a higher-spec phone might be a better shout.
You want it to look bold even in daylight
Not only is the Nord CE5’s screen a little too shiny, it also can’t quite rival flagships when it comes to outdoor peak brightness. So if you want a phone that will outshine the midday sun, maybe look elsewhere.
OnePlus Nord CE5 review: also consider

| Refresh rate | 120Hz | 120Hz | 1-120Hz (165Hz for select games) | 
| Chipset | MediaTek Dimensity 8350 Apex | Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 | Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 | 
| RAM | 8GB / 12GB (LPDDR5X) | 12GB / 16GB | 12GB / 16GB (LPDDR5X) | 
| Storage | 128GB / 256GB (UFS 3.1) | 256GB / 512GB (UFS 4.0) | 256GB / 512GB (UFS 4.1) | 
| OS | OxygenOS 15.0 (Android 15) | Redmagic OS 10 (Android 15) | OxygenOS 16.0 (Android 16) | 
| Rear cameras | 50 MP main + 8 MP ultra-wide | 50 MP main + 50 MP ultra-wide | 50 MP main + 50 MP ultra-wide + 50 MP (3.5x telephoto) | 
| Front camera | 16 MP | 16 MP (under-display) | 32 MP | 
| Battery | 5,200 mAh | 6,000 mAh | 7,300 mAh | 
| Charging | 80W SUPERVOOC wired | 80W wired | 80-100W wired, 50W wireless | 
RedMagic 10 Air
If you’re looking for a dedicated gaming phone, the RedMagic 10 Air sits right in that sweet spot between solid gaming performance and an affordable price. Costing $499 / £439 / AU$449, it offers the more powerful Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 chipset, 12GB or 16GB of RAM and a more capacious 6,000mAh battery to help you get your game on. Read our full RedMagic 10 Air review.
OnePlus 15
Should you have a little more moolah to spend, the OnePlus 15 offers all the things that make the Nord CE5 great, dialed up to flagship levels. Its top-of-the-range Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset offers staggering performance, its stunningly detailed display is capable of a 450ppi pixel density and can hit refresh rates of 165Hz, while its battery is an enormous 7,300mAh. That’s a great spec given its price starts from $899.99 / £849 (around AU$1,290). Read our full OnePlus 15 review.
How I tested the OnePlus Nord CE5
- Used it over several weeks
- Tested a broad range of features
- Have spent more than 6 years covering phones
I tested the OnePlus Nord CE5 over the course of several weeks. To assess the performance of its display, I watched multiple HDR 4K videos and compared them side-by-side with my iPhone 16 Pro to assess contrast, color and brightness. I tried the camera out in a range of contexts, from shooting flowers with a short focal range to long-distance shots using the zoom.
When weighing up the performance of its chipset, I used the phone for a range of productivity tasks in split-screen mode and played a range of demanding games on their max graphics settings. Finally, to assess battery life, I set the phone to stream a 2K video at 50% brightness for six hours to assess how long it would take to drain the entire battery.
Having covered and reviewed gadgets for more than a decade, I have a lot of experience in this area and have tested a range of phones, tablets and drawing tablets during my time at TechRadar. I’m a keen smartphone photographer, having snapped over 47,000 photos over the last 15 years — a small proportion of which I’d say are actually competently shot — and a reformed smartphone game addict who still periodically falls off the wagon.

articles.title: Qué habilidades deben aprender los diseñadores para sobrevivir en plena era de la IA
articles.text:
El auge de la inteligencia artificial está moldeando el perfil profesional de los diseñadores. La destreza técnica está quedando relegada ante la capacidad de la tecnología para generar conceptos e imágenes en segundos. Las universidades, en respuesta, han reorientado su formación: ahora buscan preparar egresados capaces de liderar la integración de sistemas inteligentes en la creación visual, en lugar de formar únicamente ejecutores de tareas técnicas. PUBLICIDAD El giro estratégico en la formación universitaria La educación superior ya no centra la discusión en restringir el uso de IA, sino en identificar cuáles competencias humanas mantendrán vigencia frente a la automatización. De acuerdo con el más reciente Future of Jobs Report del Foro Económico Mundial (WEF), el pensamiento analítico permanece como la habilidad más demandada por las empresas, mientras que la creatividad muestra el mayor ritmo de crecimiento entre las competencias valoradas. La Organización para la Cooperación y el Desarrollo Económicos (OCDE), por su parte, destaca en sus análisis que la automatización de procesos repetitivos no elimina la necesidad de talento humano, sino que desplaza el foco hacia la resiliencia, el liderazgo ético y la adaptación constante. Este cambio implica que las industrias creativas buscan profesionales capaces de asumir un rol de dirección estratégica, en lugar de limitarse a las tareas operativas. PUBLICIDAD De ejecutores a estrategas: el nuevo perfil del diseñador Eduardo Velarde, jefe académico de las carreras de Diseño de la Universidad de Ciencias y Artes de América Latina (UCAL), sostiene que la llegada de la inteligencia artificial no representa una amenaza directa para el diseñador, sino una oportunidad para elevar los estándares de la profesión. Según recoge Andina, el especialista explicó que “existe el temor de que la IA sustituirá al diseñador, cuando en realidad lo que se automatiza es únicamente la tarea técnica”. Para Velarde, el profesional del diseño debe asumir un rol directivo, como un estratega capaz de liderar sistemas, experiencias y soluciones creativas apoyadas por tecnología. PUBLICIDAD La herramienta puede entregar decenas de iteraciones en un minuto, aunque carece de contexto cultural, criterio ético y sensibilidad. Velarde plantea que la universidad debe formar profesionales capaces de formular preguntas clave, auditar los resultados algorítmicos y tomar decisiones conceptuales con impacto real. Cinco competencias clave para el futuro del diseño El escenario actual exige una redefinición de las habilidades que las universidades deben priorizar. Velarde identifica cinco ejes estratégicos para la formación de diseñadores en la era de la IA: PUBLICIDAD - Pensamiento estratégico aplicado al diseño Diagnosticar necesidades reales del mercado y de la sociedad, antes de proponer una solución visual, se vuelve esencial. Ningún algoritmo puede suplir la lectura de contexto que permite anticipar tendencias y detectar problemáticas emergentes. - Criterio creativo y curaduría El dominio del software deja de ser el principal diferencial. El profesional se define por su capacidad para curar, editar y dotar de sentido la narrativa visual, siempre alineada con el propósito de marca. La tecnología se interpreta como un asistente de producción, no como un reemplazo. PUBLICIDAD - Aprendizaje continuo y flexibilidad cognitiva El contexto tecnológico obliga a los profesionales a desarrollar la aptitud para desaprender metodologías obsoletas y asimilar nuevas herramientas de manera autónoma. La curiosidad intelectual se convierte en la principal garantía de actualización permanente. - Pensamiento crítico y responsabilidad ética La auditoría del uso de la inteligencia artificial requiere criterios sólidos en propiedad intelectual, sesgos culturales y veracidad de la información. El diseño responsable implica garantizar el respeto a la diversidad y evitar la reproducción de prejuicios automatizados. PUBLICIDAD - Visión multidisciplinaria y capacidad de adaptación La gestión de equipos heterogéneos y la habilidad para responder ante entornos de cambio acelerado se consolidan como competencias transversales. Las organizaciones valoran la capacidad para articular proyectos entre disciplinas diversas y adaptar los procesos de trabajo en función de la evolución tecnológica.

articles.title: Do you prefer analog style, liquid glass or cartoon characters on your watch? These are the 10 best Apple Watch faces of 2026 so far
articles.text:
I'm an Apple Watch die-hard — here are my picks for the 10 best Apple Watch faces of 2026 so far
Apple has some awesome Watch faces – here are my top picks
Apple makes some of the best smartwatches you can buy in 2026, especially if you're already an existing iPhone or MacBook user and embedded in Apple's ecosystem.
In many ways, the Apple Watch is Apple's most personal device, sitting right on your wrist, with plenty of color and band options – not to mention loads of different watch faces to pick from. The face you pick is where the fun really starts, as it can make the same watch feel sporty, traditional, playful, or completely different from one day to the next.
I tend to favour simpler, less complicated faces that make the time easy to read without cramming the screen with data, all of which is still available inside various apps. But I've included all sorts here. From my daily-driver Flux face to Snoopy’s wonderfully unpredictable animations, these are the 10 Apple Watch faces I’d recommend trying in 2026.
What's your favorite watch face? Let us know in the comments below!
Infograph – best Apple Watch face for complications
Infograph is the obvious pick for anyone who wants plenty of information on-screen. It supports up to eight complications, although I prefer a cleaner setup with just four fitness-focused ones in the centre.
Why it works: You can tailor it around work, exercise, weather, or everyday shortcuts, and most complications open the relevant app when tapped. Leaving a few spaces empty also makes it much easier to read at a glance.
Limitations: It can become cluttered very quickly, especially once you start mixing lots of colors and data types. If you mainly want to check the time, Infograph is probably more watch face than you need.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Flow – best Liquid Glass Apple Watch face
Flow is one of the clearest showcases for watchOS 26’s Liquid Glass design, with oversized translucent numerals set against a colorful animated background. You can switch between different colors, two typefaces, and a static or moving backdrop.
Why it works: The large numbers are easy to read, while the refraction effect gives the face much more depth when you move your wrist. Blue and purple suits the glassy look particularly well, but brighter combinations can make it feel completely different.
Limitations: There are no complications, so Flow is firmly a design-first face. Its glossy, futuristic style is also probably too bold for anyone who wants their Apple Watch to resemble a traditional watch.
California – best traditional Apple Watch face
California is the closest this list gets to a classic watch dial, mixing Roman and Arabic numerals in its most recognisable form. You can also switch between several numeral styles, use a circular or full-screen layout, and add a handful of complications.
Why it works: It gives the Apple Watch a more traditional look without losing useful extras such as the date, weather, or app shortcuts. Darker colors and restrained complications suit it especially well.
Limitations: Bright or overly detailed complications can clash with the clean dial, while the full-screen version leaves less room for information. It's also less playful than Apple’s more modern faces.
Numerals Duo – best bold digital Apple Watch face
Numerals Duo fills almost the entire screen with oversized hours and minutes, like Flow, making it one of Apple’s easiest faces to read at a glance. You can change the colors, numeral system, and choose between Filled, Hybrid, and Outline styles.
Why it works: The huge numbers give it some personality without making the time difficult to find. My multi-colored Hybrid version is especially playful, but a simpler two-color setup can look much cleaner.
Limitations: There are no complications, so you lose quick access to weather, fitness data, and so on. It is also unapologetically digital, which may not appeal if you prefer a more watch-like design.
Snoopy – best character Apple Watch face
Snoopy brings the Apple Watch to life with short animations featuring Snoopy, Woodstock, and the clock hands. The scenes change throughout the day, while different color options give the face a slightly different feel.
Why it works: The animations are really charming and varied enough to stay fun beyond the first few days. My “ARF!” scene pictured above captures the playful side of the face particularly well.
Limitations: There are no complications, and some animations briefly make the time harder to read. The Snoopy face might work best as a weekend-only option.
Flux – best dynamic digital Apple Watch face
Flux is my daily-driver face, combining oversized numerals with a block of color that rises from the bottom as each minute passes. You can switch between different colors and Western Arabic, Eastern Arabic, or Devanagari numerals.
Why it works: It is simple, bold, and immediately readable, but the constant movement stops it from feeling static. The numerals also shift into a new shape whenever the minute changes. Really cool face.
Limitations: Flux has no complications, so it only tells you the time. The unusual numeral shapes can also take a little getting used to, particularly with some color combinations.
Color – best minimalist analogue Apple Watch face
Color is a clean, flexible analogue face that can be dressed up with bright shades or kept deliberately understated. You can choose between circular and dial layouts, including a full-screen version, and then add complications or a monogram.
Why it works: It keeps the focus on the time while still leaving room for a useful shortcut or two. My full-screen version uses a single Camera Remote complication, but the circular layout can carry much more information.
Limitations: It lacks the personality of Apple’s more animated faces, and adding too many complications quickly undermines its simplicity.
Timelapse – best scenic Apple Watch face
Timelapse turns your watch into a tiny moving cityscape, with options including London, New York City, Paris, Hong Kong, Shanghai, and Mack Lake. My pick is the London version, because it's where I live, complete with Westminster and a small weather complication.
Why it works: The shifting background gives it more atmosphere than a static photo face, while the time stays easy to spot. It also feels a little more personal when you choose a location you know.
Limitations: The selection of scenes is quite limited, and readability can vary depending on the frame. There is also likely to be a higher battery drain, and it offers far less customisation than Apple’s Photos face.
Artist – best art-led Apple Watch face
Finally, Artist turns the screen into a tiny changing portrait, with the time worked directly into the illustration. Tapping the face produces a new combination, so it rarely looks exactly the same twice.
Why it works: It feels more like a small piece of digital art than a traditional watch face. The shifting faces and colors give it plenty of personality without relying on animation. A slightly offbeat, cool pick.
Limitations: There are no complications, and some combinations are easier to read than others. It is also the least practical option here if you mainly use your watch as an information hub.
How to add and customise Apple Watch faces
The easiest method is through the Watch app on your iPhone.
Open the Face Gallery, choose a design, then adjust its colors, style, numerals, and complications before tapping Add to Watch.
The available controls vary a lot: Flow mainly offers visual tweaks, while Infograph lets you change almost every piece of information on-screen, and so on.
You can also make changes directly on the watch. Touch and hold the current face, tap Edit, then swipe through the available options and turn the Digital Crown to make your selections.
How to pick the right Apple Watch face
The best place to start is with what you actually want to see when you raise your wrist. That might be nothing more than the time, or it could include your next appointment, Activity rings, weather, and a shortcut to your most-used app.
Complications are useful, but from experience, more is not always better. Too much information can make things feel cluttered, especially if you have a smaller model like my Apple Watch SE.
It's also worth setting up a few faces for different situations. You might use Infograph during the working day, switch to something fitness-focused for a workout, then move to Snoopy at the weekend.
Finally, test each face outdoors and at a quick glance – a color combination that looks great in the Watch app may be much harder to read on your wrist.

articles.title: Lista de los 10 videos en tendencia hoy en YouTube Argentina
articles.text:
Con 17 años de vida, YouTube se ha convertido en la plataforma de videos más famosa del mundo y es que en estos días no sólo sirve a los usuarios para ver clips musicales o graciosos, sino que también es empleada por muchos para ver tutoriales y aprender, para conciliar el sueño con los famosos ASMR, visitar otros países a través de diversos videobloggers y mucho más.
Aunque YouTube ha visto nacer plataformas que le han querido hacer la competencia —como Dailymotion, Vimeo y las propias redes sociales Instagram, Facebook y TikTok—, el sitio web de origen estadounidense continúa en el gusto de los internautas, lo que lo ha llevado a ser el segundo sitio más buscado sólo detrás de Google.
PUBLICIDAD
En este panorama, YouTube lanzó en el año 2018 su propia sección de tendencias en donde los usuarios pueden ver los nuevos videos musicales que gozan de gran popularidad en tiempo real en 61 países, ello con la finalidad de que no se pierdan ninguno de los clips más importantes, pues se estima que cada minuto son subidos más de 500 horas de contenido mientras que al día son vistos alrededor de 5 mil millones de videos.
Aquí el listado de los 10 artistas y sus canciones más populares del momento
1. Te viArtista/canal: La Joaqui y Callejero Fino
2. torpe (Official Video)Artista/canal: Ángela Torres
3. Partido En DosArtista/canal: Daniel Agostini y The La Planta
4. 90s (Official Video)Artista/canal: Trueno y Maria Becerra
5. Anuel AA | Donde Hubo Fuego Cenizas Quedan (Video Oficial)Artista/canal: Anuel AA
6. FronteoArtista/canal: Plan B
7. Encantadora (Remix)Artista/canal: Yandel
8. Tu Falta De Querer (En Vivo)Artista/canal: Eugenia Quevedo
9. Pa Mí (Remix)Artista/canal: Dalex
10. This & ThatArtista/canal: Stray Kids
Los inicios de YouTube
YouTube vio la luz en febrero de 2005, cuando tres antiguos empleados de la compañía de Paypal ―Chad Hurley, Steve Chen y Jawed Karim― se unieron y la crearon luego de que experimentaran dificultades para compartir entre sí un par de videos tras asistir a una fiesta.
PUBLICIDAD
El dominio fue activado el 14 de febrero de 2005 y casi un mes después, el 23 de abril, fue cargado el primer clip a la plataforma que llevaba por nombre “Me at the Zoo”. Fue cuestión de tiempo para que todo el mundo comenzara a cargar contenido y a compartir los enlaces a través de otras redes sociales como MySpace.
Una de las grandes empresas que vio el potencial de YouTube fue la marca Nike, que subió una publicidad protagonizada por Ronaldinho, lo que hizo que otras grandes compañías voltearan a ver a YouTube y se sintieran atraídas.
PUBLICIDAD
Tal fue la gran acogida de los internautas por YouTube que para diciembre de 2005 la plataforma pasó de las 50 millones de visitas al día a 250 millones de visualizaciones luego de que un canal subiera el clip musical Lazy Sunday, transmitido originalmente por Saturday Night Live.
Para el año siguiente, en el 2006, el sitio fue comparado por el gigante del internet, Google, por un valor de 1650 millones de dólares. En ese entonces eran visualizados 100 millones de videos al día y 65 mil clips se añadían a diario. También firmaron acuerdos con disqueras para poder reproducir videos musicales.
PUBLICIDAD
YouTube en la cultura popular
Desde que fue puesto en marcha, YouTube fue un sitio que llegó a hacer una revolución no sólo en internet, sino también en la forma en la que los usuarios miran contenido. Muestra de ello el reconocimiento que la revista Time le otorgó en noviembre del 2006 al ser nombrado el “Invento del Año”.
Convertido en el mejor medio de difusión, el gozar de tanta popularidad también ha metido a sus dueños en aprietos como cuando albergar peleas escolares o en donde hay bullying, clips relacionados al terrorismo, narcotráfico u otros temas considerados delicados por su contenido íntimo o por mostrar delitos como asesinatos y más.
PUBLICIDAD
Para Estados Unidos uno de los temas más delicados es el de los tiroteos escolares, por lo que YouTube ha estado más de una vez en el ojo del huracán por alojar contenido filmado por los atacantes, como fue el caso de la masacre de Virginia Tech, cuando Cho Seung-Hui, el atacante, subió previamente a los hechos un discurso.
Más recientemente, tras el surgimiento de la pandemia del coronavirus, también ha surgido inquietud sobre cómo la plataforma permite la monetización de contenido que puede ser engañoso y riesgoso para la población.
PUBLICIDAD
Aunque no todo es malo, pues a través de dicha plataforma muchas personas han podido ser reconocidas por su talento, como fue el caso de Susan Boyle, quien participó en el programa Britain’s Got Talent cuyo extracto subido a YouTube logró que la mujer pasara a ser una completa desconocida a una de las personas más viralizadas, famosas y aclamadas del internet.
